classification.difficultyReason: Connects polynomial roots and their sum with the geometry of line–curve intersections.

content.prompt: When the equation of a line is substituted into the equation of a curve, a polynomial equation $P(x)=0$ is obtained.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What do the roots of $P(x)=0$ represent geometrically?

answer.short: The real roots are the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points of the line and the curve.
answer.worked: Substitution eliminates $y$. Each real root gives an $x$-value satisfying both equations; substituting this value into the line gives the corresponding $y$-coordinate. Thus the real roots are the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the sum of the roots is zero, what does this imply geometrically about their positions?

answer.short: If all roots are real, their mean $x$-coordinate is zero, counting repeated roots according to multiplicity. With two real roots, the intersection points are horizontally equally spaced on either side of the $y$-axis, or both roots are zero. A zero sum alone does not imply pairwise symmetry for more roots.
answer.worked:
If the roots $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are all real, counting multiplicity,
$$\begin{align*}\bar{x}&=\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}\\\bar{x}&=0.\end{align*}$$
Their mean horizontal position is therefore on the $y$-axis. For two real roots, $x_2=-x_1$, so the intersections have opposite $x$-coordinates. For more roots, a zero sum need not give pairwise symmetry: for example, $-3,1,2$ sum to zero. If some roots are non-real, the sum of all roots alone does not determine the mean horizontal position of the real intersections.
